paragraphs.text: Every day is bright, bearing the ray of the sun and adorned with the light common to all. For so the Master beautified creation and brought it into being. But a festal day, solemn and wholly festive, honored with the word and worship of God, holds more for gladness. It displays a twofold beauty, bearing the bloom of nature and showing the loveliness of piety. Such is today's feast: it shines upon the bodily eye of sense, and it lights up the inward eye of the mind with the rays of the word.

For today is one of the three great feasts, proclaimed in the Law and sung through the grace of the Gospel. On this day, under the old covenant, the Law was given. On this day, under the new grace, the coming of the Spirit was given. On this day Moses received the tablets of the Law. On this day the choir of the apostles received the descent of the Spirit, in place of the tablets given through Moses. For the blessed Paul says, writing in his letter to the Corinthians: "You are our letter, written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the heart, tablets of flesh." But you ask whether the Law was truly given on this day. For it is not expressly written in the Old Testament that the Law was given at Pentecost; yet for those who search the divine writings a treasure of knowledge comes to light.

Let us see, then, on what day the Law was given. For the blessed Moses says (so pay close attention): "In the third month after they had gone out of the land of Egypt, the Lord said to Moses: Go down and charge the people, and they shall purify themselves today and tomorrow, and on the third day I will appear." Pay close attention. The exodus from Egypt was in the first month; it was the fourteenth of the first month. Take the fourteenth day, and after it the days that complete the month, that is, seventeen, and the thirty days of the second month. And on the forty-eighth day, of the second month, God said: "Charge the people today and tomorrow, and on the third day of the month I will appear." So: thirty of the second month, seventeen of the first, and three of the third.

And see how the events agree. When God appeared on Mount Sinai, he appeared as a burning fire. When the Holy Spirit appeared to the apostles, he appeared in the form of fire: for "tongues as of fire were distributed, and one rested on each of them." And just as, brothers, when God appeared under the old covenant there were many terrors escorting him (for darkness and storm and trumpet and thunder surrounded the mountain, to prepare the people to fear the Lawgiver), so too when the Holy Spirit was about to come, in order that the suddenness of his arrival might not lead those receiving him into carelessness, but that they might learn the dignity of the Spirit coming upon them, then, just as darkness and storm went before on the mountain, so it happened with the Spirit as well. "When the day of Pentecost was being fulfilled, there came a sound as of a violent rushing wind." And then the Holy Spirit appeared and shook the house, being distributed not in his nature, but distributing his workings.

For the Spirit is not divided; rather he divides the gifts, as Paul testifies: "All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, dividing to each individually as he wills": dividing, not divided; distributing, not distributed; exercising authority, not subject to authority. And the honor of authority that Paul gave to the Father when he said, "It is God who works all things in all," he expressed in the same words of the Spirit as well, saying: "All these," he says, "are worked by one and the same Spirit." But the Holy Spirit was called the Paraclete. Why, if not because he exhorts people, that is, comforts them? You will find this usage in Scripture: the apostle calls comfort "exhortation." And he exhorts not as one second to God, but as God. For exhorting is proper to God. For the apostle says, so that you may not insult the title "Paraclete": "We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us."

And so that, brothers, Paul may not be thought to bring novelty into doctrine by presenting God as exhorting people, take proof from ancient testimony. Isaiah the prophet says to Jerusalem: "He who named you will comfort you." The Father comforts you; the Son comforts. For he says: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to comfort all who mourn." Moreover, the Savior, wishing to show the Spirit's equal glory, says: "When I go away, I will send another Paraclete." But there could be no "another" unless someone else had been placed first.

So the Holy Spirit appears in the form of tongues of fire. Why tongues, then? Because of their usefulness for preaching. Since the apostles needed a tongue in order to fill the ends of the world through their preaching, what the Holy Spirit was going to work is given shape in the gift. And besides, it was because of an ancient event. For once, when the giants fought against God and wanted to build a tower, God sent tongues and split the concord of the wicked; now too he sends the working of tongues, to join together the divided world. And it was a strange thing: tongues cut the world apart; tongues joined the world together, tongues for the sake of preaching. But why of fire? Because impiety had run wild like a forest and held the whole world bound fast like thorns, he sends fiery tongues to consume the thorns of impiety. For he it is who says: "I came to cast fire upon the earth." A fire that does not destroy; for the fire of God does not burn but sanctifies. That is why one of the cherubim was sent to Isaiah holding a coal of fire from the altar. And when he laid it on his lips, he said to him: "Behold, I have taken away your iniquities and your sins."

So, as we reverently celebrate this feast of the coming of the Holy Spirit, let us send up glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Honor the coming of the Spirit. And the coming of the Spirit is honored in the forgiveness of sins. For where the Holy Spirit is, there is remission. For the Lord says: "Receive the Holy Spirit; if you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven them." The Holy Spirit proclaims what sets free. That is: the Father sets free, the Son sets free, the Holy Spirit sets free. But a slave cannot grant freedom, for he does not give what he does not have. Therefore, so that you may learn the new freedom of the Son and of the Spirit, the Savior says of himself: "Unless the Son sets you free, you are slaves." He ascribed freedom to himself. Again Paul says: "So we behold as in a mirror, as from the Lord, the Spirit; for the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Sometimes he is called the Holy Spirit, sometimes the Spirit of the Son, sometimes the Spirit of the Father; this is not proclaimed in confusion, but expresses the indivisibility of the divine essence. The Son calls him the Spirit of the Father: "Do not worry," he says, "about what you will say; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of the Father." The Son speaks of the Spirit of the Father; Paul speaks of the Spirit of the Son. For he says this: "Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, 'Abba, Father.'" The Spirit also gives life. For he says: "Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills." You have seen the Father and the Son giving life. But look again at the apostle, or rather at the Savior himself speaking through him: "It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh is of no benefit."

I will speak more briefly still. Ordinations in the churches are attributed by Paul sometimes to the Father, sometimes to the Son, and sometimes to the Spirit. For instance, when he speaks of the Father appointing the ranks in the Church, he says: "God has set in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers," and so on. Here he attributed the appointments to the Father, because it is he who has authority and appoints. Elsewhere, again, the same Paul attributes them to the Son. For he says: "He who descended is the same one who ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things; and he gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some pastors and teachers." See the authority in the word. He did not say, "And he assisted," but "He gave," by his own authority, while the kingdom of the Father is not divided and split apart. For what the Father wills, the Son also wills, and what the Son wills, the Father also approves. So the same apostle again ascribes to the Holy Spirit the appointments that he attributed to the Father and to the Son, when he summons the elders of Ephesus and says to them (Paul, who said those things, also utters these): "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has set you as overseers, to shepherd the Church." See how the wording agrees. He did not say "he established" of the Father and "he arranged" of the Spirit, but used the same word: God the Father "set" in the Church; the Holy Spirit "set" in the Church. The Father legislates in the Church. The Father legislates as King of the ages, of whom David says: "I desired to do your will, O my God, and your law is in the midst of my heart." So the Father legislates, and the Son legislates. Hear Paul saying: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." He has shown the Father legislating; he has shown the Son legislating. The same apostle, giving to the Holy Spirit too the dignity of lawgiving, or rather not giving it but rendering it as his due, says: "For the law of the Spirit of life has set me free in Christ Jesus." Not that there are three lawgivers. For there is one law and one Lawgiver; one God, even though he is proclaimed in three persons.

"And how," someone says, "can the Father be called God, and the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, and yet not three gods?" Where the things of nature are shared, the names of dignity are shared too. For example, God calls by one name things that are divided into multitudes but come from a single nature. When he is angry with humans, he calls the whole of humankind that is subject to his wrath one man. And when he is reconciled to the world, he speaks as to one man. For instance, God brings a flood because of sins and says: "My Spirit shall not remain among these men. I will blot out man, whom I have made." And yet there was not one, but countless myriads. But by the name of their nature he called them all as one, the whole world as one man, because their essence is shared. "What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?" says David. Not that he visited one; for he raised up the whole world. I will use one brief saying spoken through Moses, when Pharaoh went out toward the sea and paid the penalty to the divine law. Pharaoh falls into the sea with countless chariots. And many men were sunk with him, and many horses. But Moses, knowing that the nature of all humans is one, says: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea." The multitudes of men he named one rider, because they share one essence.

If, then, among human beings, where knowledge is confused and the forms of their appearance differ (for they are not one, nor of one mind, but have different languages and different speech), the whole world is called one man because of their common nature, then where the dignity is undivided, one kingdom, one power that is properly its own, I call the Trinity one God. But if, by saying God and God and God, I speak of three gods, then if I say Lord and Lord and Lord, do I speak of three lords? By no means. For the apostle calls the Father Lord, the Son Lord, and the Holy Spirit Lord. As David also says: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand." See: Lord to Lord. The apostle says: "Now the Lord is the Spirit." If, then, the Father is Lord, and the Son Lord, and the Spirit Lord, how is it, O apostle, lawgiver of truth, advocate of piety, that you cry out to the Ephesians, saying: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism"? One Lord, in keeping with the hymn of holiness of the seraphim; for they cry out: "Holy, holy, holy Lord." But if the heretics insist that the lordship of the Father is one thing and that of the Son another, I wonder how they can bear to serve two lords. For it is the Savior's saying: "No one can serve two lords." If you divide the authority, how do you serve the kingdom? For two dignities cannot be worshiped together unless they are equal in honor. No one does homage to the king and to a governor alike. Where the dignity is equal in honor, the worship is equal in honor too. In equal dignity there is no strife. Inequality stirs up strife; equality presides over peace. Christ did not permit you to divide the honor. For he says: "This is the will of the Father, that all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father." Honor the Father, so that you may honor the Son; or rather, honor the Son, so that you may honor the Father. The Father makes the Son's honor his own; the Son makes the Father's honor his own. For the Savior says: "Whoever hates me hates my Father also."

So let the heretics not suppose that they are doing God a favor by calling him greater than the Son. For the Father does not accept honor offered to him while the Son is insulted. And take a clear proof from events in the Old Scripture. Job's friends, who had come to console him, accused him of speaking boldly, and they justified God. But Job said to God: "Who will grant me an arbiter between me and you, so that I may know how many are my sins, that you have judged me in this way?" Job's friends justified God without knowing the matter; they rather condemned the righteous man as a sinner, and pleaded God's case as the one who had brought the affliction. And they say to him: "You have spoken grandly, you have spoken beyond measure against the Mighty One; does God pervert what is just? He brought this on you according to your sins. If your sins were not many, you would not have been scourged." And they thought they were advocates for God, but they condemned the righteous man. Did God accept those who spoke on his behalf contrary to justice? If he accepted advocacy on his behalf while the righteous man was dishonored, then he also accepts honor to himself while the Son is dishonored. Hear what the Lord says to Job's friends: "Why have you not spoken rightly against my servant?" If he rejects those who did not speak rightly against his servant, will he accept one who sharpens his tongue against the Only-begotten? Far from it!

There is no escape, then, from judgment for those who blaspheme the Holy Spirit. Hear what the Savior says: "Every blasphemy will be forgiven men, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come." What need is there of syllogisms about begotten and unbegotten, created and uncreated? The argument of heresy is sharper than a whetted razor. But a razor, however greatly and strongly sharpened, can shave hairs, but cannot cut wood. The word of truth is not a razor but an axe. That is why John the Baptist says: "Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the trees." He did not say a razor. For it is not smooth, like those who smooth over their emptiness on the outside with words. Rather, the word of God is an axe that cuts down the arrogance of the boastful, as John testifies, saying: "Even now the axe is laid at the root of the trees." The crowd of those who speak deceit and weave heresies is a razor, as David says to Saul: "Why do you boast in wickedness, you who are mighty in iniquity? All day long your tongue has devised injustice; like a sharpened razor you have worked deceit." The Father legislates; the Son commands; the Spirit exercises authority.

Hear God saying: "Those whom the Lord has called will come bringing good news." I beg you, lend me your ear, so that you may learn how the truth agrees with itself. For we do not do battle with reasonings, but follow the Scriptures. We pray to be servants of the Scriptures, not to make the Scriptures slaves to our own reasonings. Faith does not admit syllogisms, not because it is irrational, but because it surpasses all reasoning. And to show you that faith is armed against reasonings, Paul says: "For our weapons are not fleshly, but powerful before God for the demolition of strongholds, as we demolish reasonings and every height that raises itself against the knowledge of God." But even if the lawless man often wins by dialectic, do not be surprised. For David says: "The words of the lawless have overpowered us." The Father sends the apostles; the Son also sends them; the Holy Spirit also sends them. The Savior says to the apostles: "Behold, I send you into the world; go and make disciples of all nations." And it says in the Acts of the Apostles: "So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia." The Father calls apostles; the Son calls apostles. The prophet says: "For from Mount Zion will come the one who brings good news, and those bringing good news whom the Lord has called." So it belongs to God to call those who bring good news. If, then, calling belongs to God, that is why the Spirit, speaking through the prophets, said: "Thus says the Holy Spirit: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them." This is enough from us on these matters.

May the God of peace make us all grow in his faith and love, for to him belong all glory, honor and worship, with his only-begotten Son and his all-holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
